# The Various Stages of the Spiritual Experience: An Integrated Understanding that Will Elevate All Religions

**Author:** William Bodri
**Year:** 2002 or 2003 — see Provenance note
**Publisher:** Top Shape Publishing, Reno, Nevada (self-published)
**Original file:** `RAW/books/bodri-various-stages-of-the-spiritual-experience.md` — 37,453 lines · 470,799 words · 673 PDF pages
**Source type:** practitioner (secondary character: comparative-religion synthesis)

---

## Core Argument

Every genuine spiritual tradition is climbing the same ladder, and the ladder is checkable. Bodri takes five schemes from Mahāyāna Buddhism, Taoism and Yogācāra — the five paths, the jing-chi-shen transformation sequence, the five skandhas, the four dhyāna and four formless absorptions, and the eight consciousnesses — and argues they describe one process from five angles. He then uses that composite grid to rank what the world's religions actually deliver, and the verdict is severe: almost everything called spirituality, including bhakti, rosary, dervish dancing, visualisation, prāṇāyāma, mantra and prayer, lands in the two preparatory stages before anyone has seen the Tao at all. His warrant for the whole enterprise is that the physical transformations of cultivation are nondenominational and observable, so an attainment claim can be tested against a body rather than accepted on authority.

---

## Key Contributions

- **A composite cross-tradition grid** for locating any reported spiritual state, built by matching phenomenon against phenomenon rather than term against term — with an explicit criterion stated for doing so (*compare gong-fu, not dogma*), which the book's own practice frequently violates.
- **A sustained catalogue of counterfeit attainment** — semblance dharmas, dead-tree Zen, dry wisdom, frozen-ice practice, the *du-yin* shadow consciousness, the error of naturalism — each with a named mechanism and a stated tell.
- **The falsifiability keystone:** physical transformations are a precondition of, not decoration on, claimed stages; if the marks do not appear, the stage was not reached.
- **Three annotated first-person case studies** — Robert Forman's "tubes," U. G. Krishnamurti's calamity, and Yin Shih Tsu's eight-channel record — each re-described line by line in Taoist biophysics.
- **A decoding method applied across five symbolic systems** — maṇḍala directions, Tantric vocabulary, the *tu mai* / *jen mai* channels, *Journey to the West*, and the Six Yogas — resolving each into the eight-consciousness scheme. In every case the practice survives the decoding and the mystique does not.
- **The Gampopa narrative** — eighteen episodes of vision and diagnosis under Milarepa, the only sustained record in the book of a teacher reading a student's states in real time, and the source of its most humbling deflation: a hell-vision caused by a tight meditation belt.
- **An institutional analysis** running underneath the cultivation material: how a tradition's ceiling is set by whoever codified it first, why organisations suppress the practices that would free adherents from needing them, and why supremacy claims are structurally forced on any school that wants to survive.
- **Two further places where the book caps its own product, both one line long and both in low-status structural positions.** At **p 526**, in a chapter summary: *"The concentration of this book is on seeing the Tao, which is realizing the dharmakaya"* — **the first of three components, by the author's own statement**, and the warrant for the vault's standing rule that no page presents this as a complete path. At **p 620**, in an exhortation: *"all the talk about kundalini, chi mai and chakras and clear light, jing-chi-shen, heavens, omnipresent mental functions, skandhas, samadhi and so on is essentially unnecessary because the real Tao is just about behavior … the measure of mastering the Tao is your inner and outer behavior."* ⚑ **These yield a structural reading the book does not make: the practice it actually recommends is defined as having no session boundary — *"true meditation which you're supposed to be in at all times," "not a practice itself, but nonpractice of unnecessary mental habits"* — so it has no unit and nothing to report, and behaviour is the only measurement instrument that fits it. The closing ethical chapters are the assessment scheme, not a coda.**
- **A second decline mechanism, distinct from the codifier-ceiling one at p 421.** A scheme built simple for a lay audience acquires practices, then a *medical* structure, then everyday users who never cultivated — after which *"it became difficult to drop this scheme even after other higher explanations were available, and it had lost its early usefulness."* **A framework held by its believers' convictions dies with them; a framework held by the dependencies built on top of it has no cohort whose death would release it.**
- **A structural finding about transmission failure, arrow reversed from the eightfold-path case.** The no-leakage rule is **two-part** — retention *and* mental emptiness — and **all four traditional names for it designate only the enforceable half.** What survives in the vocabulary is what a community can police.
- **A four-wisdom transformation scheme (p 468) that is the only *transformational* map in the book**, and therefore its own best answer to the worry it states repeatedly that emptiness will be read as annihilation: eight consciousnesses convert into four wisdoms, nothing is deleted, and the seventh — the faculty whose entire function was insisting on a separate self — becomes the Universal Equality Wisdom through which the saṃbhogakāya is manifested. ⚠ **The mandala assignment gives four Buddhas and four compass points and never pairs each Buddha with its wisdom;** *"accordingly"* asserts an ordering the passage does not supply.
- **A footnote (518, p 511) that disclaims the book's own apparatus** — the stages are "false stages," the *Śūraṅgama* teaches enlightenment "without stages at all," and the whole scheme is offered as rest stops, verifications and motivational assists rather than as a necessary route.

---

## The Two Reading Rules

*Both established across the full 673-page read and both at `[n≥3 PATTERN]`. They govern how everything below is used and they are the most portable findings about this source.*

**1. Bodri is careful, hedged and specific on contemplative phenomenology, and confident and wrong wherever he borrows external authority.** The two registers are separable, they are separable *by topic*, and the failure is not distributed randomly. Documented instances: the non-local consciousness claim, where the footnote says a third of what the sentence says (pp 144, 432) · the Jung characterisation, which misstates the evidence base of the framework it rejects (p 422) · the Wright brothers and Edison history, sourced to Richard Milton's *Alternative Science* and substantially untrue (p 347, fn 303) · the claim that the ancient sciences of India, China and Egypt "came about through the investigations of those with samādhi attainments" (p 331), unsourced and contradicted by the documented development of those bodies of knowledge · Lincoln waiting until the time was right to free the slaves (p 647), one contested reading of a contested record, in a subordinate clause · and Gandhi devising non-violence because he lacked guns (p 649), where the attributed remark has a real basis in his writing on cowardice and violence but **the causal claim is Bodri's own, unsourced, and contradicted by the bulk of that writing.**

> **Operating rule: take the practice descriptions seriously and verify every historical or scientific assertion independently. The instances cluster where he is annexing somebody else's material to make a point.**

**2. His best evidence appears as a list item and his weakest gets an argument.** The nine-tradition convergence on a *technique* (p 428) is one sentence — and it is far stronger evidence than any state-concordance, because a technique has to be practised to be transmitted and a description does not. Deikman's clinically-derived observing self, the only genuinely independent corroboration in the book, is a list entry with no engagement. Against which the four-column state concordance, which is vulnerable to borrowing in exactly the way a technique is not, gets a chapter. The same shape recurs structurally: **his load-bearing arguments arrive in subordinate clauses and his taxonomies get chapters** — the bypass claim (one sentence, p 157) · the two-criterion test for judging any tradition's scheme (one sentence, p 429) · the ālaya-indifference derivation, the only specification in the book shown to *follow* from anything (one sentence, p 473) · and the claim that the absorptions are reachable because the seeds giving access to them are *shared*, which is the mechanism for the entire nondenominational thesis (half a sentence, p 492, never returned to).

> **Operating rule: when reading this book, the argument is not where the space is.**

---

## Limitations

**Classification rationale.** This is a practitioner text, not a scholarly one. Bodri writes as a cultivation teacher in a named lineage — the student of Nan Huai-Chin — and his authority for the book's central claims is his own asserted attainment. He states this plainly and, to his credit, refuses to treat his own testimony as evidence for the reader: *"My saying it is so because of my own experiences is no proof for you."* He also concedes the book is a compression of "nearly four thousand" other books, and says it was written to the shape of an imagined university course.

**The citation chain is the main limitation.** Bodri does not read the primary texts to the reader; he reads translators' and anthologists' renderings of them. Every claim drawn from this book must be attributed as *Bodri citing [the intermediary] citing [the text]*, never as the text directly. Four intermediaries carry most of the load: Nan Huai-Chin, Thomas and J.C. Cleary, Lu K'uan Yu, and the Bihar School *Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā*.

**The Forman dependency.** A single 1990 academic anthology — Robert K. C. Forman's *The Problem of Pure Consciousness* — supplies a large share of the non-Asian mystical citations, including the Stace material, the Kabbalistic *ayin* passages, the *ex nihilo* / *ex Deo* formula and the three-fold selflessness gloss. The book's apparent breadth across Western mysticism is substantially one shelf. Bodri makes the selection principle explicit in a footnote, recommending Daniel Matt over Gershom Scholem for the Kabbalah *because* Matt emphasises the pursuit of *ayin* — which is what his argument needs.

**And the dependency has now been measured at its point of maximum load.** Across **pp 479–488 — ten pages — five of the non-Asian witnesses to the *neither something nor nothing* convergence come from Forman, and four of the five from a fifteen-page span of him**: the Christian *ex nihilo = ex Deo* formula (fn 470, Forman p 126) · Pseudo-Dionysius (fn 476, p 153) · the Shi'i Ismāʿīlī unity (fn 478, p 126) · the *Sefer Yezirah* passage (fn 482, p 132) · Maimonides on description by negation (fn 488, p 127). Whole-book count of Forman citations: **21.** ⚑ **This matters more here than anywhere else in the book because the argument being supported is a *convergence* argument, and the entire force of a convergence argument is the independence of its witnesses.** A thematic anthology assembled by a scholar arguing a thesis about pure consciousness delivers a sample **selected on the dependent variable**, and reading five passages off consecutive pages of it double-counts that selection. **The finding the citations will bear is: *apophatic strands exist across these traditions, and a scholar who set out to collect apophatic strands found them in all of these places.*** That is real and it is much weaker than five independent witnesses. **One counter-instance bounds it on the same pages: Plotinus is cited at fn 477 by internal *Enneads* locator rather than through an anthology.**

**A second and structurally identical failure, arriving by the opposite route — the Jesus Sutras at p 570.** Bodri cites Church of the East texts from Tang-dynasty China as independent corroboration that the *prāṇa*/Winds account of death is cross-traditional. **The Jesus Sutras were written in Taoist Chinese by translators working inside a Chinese religious vocabulary, centuries after that vocabulary existed** — so the dependency runs *from* the Taoist material *into* the Christian text, which dissolves the convergence rather than supporting it. **Where the Forman witnesses were selected by a modern scholar with a thesis, this witness was written in the terminology it is cited as confirming.**

**The compendium-citation habit.** Named Sanskrit texts are repeatedly located in compendia from another tradition or genre: the *Avadhūta Gītā* and the *Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā* cited to a *Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā* volume, a Chinese Ch'an master cited to a book on natural Tantra, a Chuang Tzu passage cited to a volume of Sufi wisdom, an Islamic ḥadīth cited to a Kabbalah anthology. What is established is that the footnotes locate texts this way; what is *not* established, and must not be asserted, is that those compendia lack the passages. One counter-instance bounds the habit: Plotinus is cited by internal *Enneads* locator.

**Body/footnote attribution mismatch — `[n=7]`, and five of the seven resolve to one volume.** This is **distinct from the compendium habit above and worse**: there the intermediary is disclosed, here **the body text credits a source the footnote contradicts.** The instances: *Hatharatnavali* → footnoted to the Bihar School *Haṭha Yoga Pradīpikā* p 370 (p 95, fn 62) · Svoboda's *Aghora* → David Gordon White, *The Alchemical Body* p 201 (p 129, fn 95) · **Patañjali's definition of prāṇāyāma** → Bihar *Pradīpikā* p 135 (p 167, fn 127) · *Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā* → Bihar *Pradīpikā* p 140 (p 168, fn 130) · *Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā* again → Bihar *Pradīpikā* p 155 (p 409, fn 374) · *Cūḍāmaṇi Upaniṣad* → Bihar *Pradīpikā* p 308 (p 586, fn 592) · and *"as the Netra Tantra in Hinduism says"* → **Kṣemarāja's *Pratyabhijñāhṛdayam***, trans. Jaideva Singh, SUNY 1990, p 63 (p 558, fn 560), with the caveat that Kṣemarāja is also the *Netra Tantra*'s commentator, so the intermediary is plausible there. **Four separately named Sanskrit texts all resolve to Muktibodhananda's single Bihar School edition.** It bites hardest in the yoga chapters, where the argument is a claim about *what the yoga tradition really teaches*. **A candidate eighth is recorded and not counted** — Patañjali credited in the body at p 179 fn 141 with Feuerstein's *The Philosophy of Yoga* p 104 in the note — because Feuerstein's volume is a study of the sūtras rather than an unrelated compendium.

**A further sub-species, `[n=1 OBSERVED]`: translator's commentary quoted as scripture.** At p 485 a block is introduced as *"As the Awakening of Faith says"* and footnoted to Hakeda pp 32–38. The block contains a sentence dating Nāgārjuna for modern readers — it is **Hakeda's commentary, not the śāstra**, and the *intrinsic / accidental* formula that a vault page is named after sits inside it. **Mitigated and not counted with the mismatch pattern**, because he cites the same sentence correctly as *"the commentary"* at p 501. The handling rule: anyone quoting p 485 alone will get it wrong.

**Top Shape Publishing self-citation — `[n=3]`.** Three load-bearing quotations are sourced to Nan Huai-Chin volumes published by **Bodri's own publisher**: the channel/nerve identification that is the book's most load-bearing physiological claim (p 409, *The Story of Chinese Taoism*, trans. William Brown, Top Shape, Reno, 2002) · the *hun tun* cosmogony (p 177, fn 138, same volume) · and the *Classic of Purity and Stillness* block (p 528, fn 540, same volume, **with no page number given**). Recorded as a source-integrity note, not as an allegation.

**Bracketed interpolation — `[n≥5]`.** Bodri prints **his own comparative reading inside the source's sentence, in square brackets**, rather than stating it after the quotation. Disclosed by the brackets and therefore not concealment; the cost is that a reader loses the ability to hear the source alone. Instances: Mencius p 202 (*[So how can chi-gong… help you?]*) · Motoyama p 163 · Katz's Kung healers p 166 (*[the raw kundalini energy]*) · Schauberger p 177 · the Osiris retelling p 171, where three glosses carry the entire cultivation reading · throughout the Mullin block quote pp 555–557 · Lao Tzu at p 480 (*the Tao that can be spoken **(realized)** is not the true Tao*) · Tsong Khapa at p 554 (*[this is dry Zen or dead Zen, a stage of clear equanimity without the circulation of the vital force]*) · and **the Hasidic Baal Shem Tov chain at p 552 (*[because he had samadhi]*), where the interpolation carries Bodri's entire reading of a story that, read plainly, says something different** — forms lost across four generations with the result preserved. ⚠ **Two cautions: the brackets in the Yin Shih Tsu case at pp 181–186 are the translator's, not Bodri's; and the ascending four-bliss name-assignments at p 557 are Bodri's gloss and not Tsong Khapa's** — do not attribute without checking Mullin.

**Anonymous-teacher pattern — `[n=5]`.** A teaching is quoted and attributed only to an unnamed figure in the body while the footnote supplies the name — including Tolle at p 465, where the body calls *The Power of Now* "a misleading teaching at that" and footnote 450 reads, in full, *Eckhart Tolle.* ⚑ **A correction is recorded against this count**: the p 193 U. G. Krishnamurti quotation is **not** an instance, since he is named at p 204; an over-claim of `[n=6]` was written and corrected in the same session.

**Announced count against printed count — `[n=4]`, sample size stated and no stronger.** The Tibetan five-factor etiology announces five and enumerates six · the five-element catalogue announces five and lists four, fire removed by the author's own note · the five-element scheme is underwritten by a **six**-factor *Śālistamba* passage quoted whole and unremarked (p 163) · and p 564's *"the most important of the four elements is actually the fifth element"* — **which reads as deliberate rhetoric rather than error and weakens its membership in the set.** Recorded with that caveat.

**Named self-contradictions beyond the four positions listed below.** Each is carried on the relevant page rather than resolved. **p 250** (*cause and effect are not different, the beginning and end interpenetrate*) against **pp 464–467**'s hard cause-level / effect-level split — p 250 concedes the split is *conventional*, which downgrades the verdict it certifies. **The wave image printed twice, with the conditional clause *only if you refrain from providing them with any further energy* present at p 248 and absent at p 574** — and the version that travels as the cross-tradition invariant is the one with the instruction stripped off. **p 97** describes the chi channels as a *separate* system with independent scientific verification claimed, against **p 409**'s flat identification of them *with* the nervous system — the first claim requires the second to be false. **p 121** (*they happen to everybody… no matter whether they are male or female*) against **p 123**'s three-way branch by sex and age. **p 165 vs p 179** — the five-element ladder's year-counts require each element to finish before the next begins, against *people always end up going through multiple cycles*; **staircase against spiral, neither withdrawn.** **p 176 vs p 564** — *empty space doesn't have the same meaning as mental emptiness. Both have to be cultivated* against the p 564 sentence that begins with the space element and ends with the occupiable state; **load-bearing, since it is the joint on which the central mind-to-body instruction hangs.** **p 504** — *"we actually gain omniscience"* and *"it's not that we know everything"*, two sentences apart, **with the retracted strong claim then spent as evidence at p 505.** **p 468** — the Esoteric school *typically* represents the four wisdoms in mandalas, and two clauses later *"most spiritual schools never tell you about these lofty matters because they don't reach very high."*

**Two incompatible partitions of one stage, never reconciled.** p 542 divides the tantric completion stage six ways **by faculty** (three isolations, three arrivals); pp 553–555 divides the same stage six ways **by technique**, following the Six Yogas of Naropa, with inner heat as the declared foundation. Both are Tibetan, both are credited to Tsong Khapa, and they are eleven pages apart. **This is the easiest correspondence the book's comparative method will ever face — same tradition, same century, same named authority — and it is the only one not attempted**, in a passage that names the difficulty of drawing such correspondences and then skips it.

**Verification gated on prior acceptance.** The book's epistemology has a standing circularity, stated four separate times. The eight-consciousness taxonomy is said to be visible only from inside the first dhyāna; "sentient matter" is posited as necessary, undiscovered by science, and verifiable only by those who have already reached the samādhi blisses; the Consciousness-Only teachings "totally rely on proof" that can be had only by cultivating correctly, where correctness is defined by the system; and critics who have not meditated are said to "lack any qualifications to even be commenting upon these matters." The counterweight noted above — his refusal to treat his own experience as proof — makes this an unstable position rather than a simple one.

**"The explanation is in the untranslated book."** Three times, for claims the reader has no other way to check, the mechanism is said to be explained in Yen-shou's *Source Mirror*, which Bodri notes is not available in English.

**Author self-positioning.** Three first-person lineage claims function as authority claims about the author in a book whose argument is that authority claims must be checkable: a grandmaster who dispels a temple full of lights by shouting at them; a transmission after three kowtows, where his teacher said that in decades of teaching thousands he had never found anyone else to whom he could transmit it; and "This I have personally witnessed on many occasions."

**Unsupported evaluative sweeps.** National and ethnic character claims appear three times. Living traditions are dismissed wholesale in a clause three times — most shamanic practice worldwide, "the scholars who write about Zen," and "Japanese Zen practice today" — each unsourced and unengaged. Targets are frequently unnamed, though in one instance the refusal to name is declared rather than concealed.

**Indigenous traditions are handled at a distance.** Across seven instances the pattern is annexation as corroboration or dismissal as inferior — !Kung *num* and *kia* read as crude forced chi circulation, Native American trickster stories and peyote claimed for the yang-shen mechanism, a Hopi four-chakra scheme asserted without source, most shamanic technique classed as demonic, and "the land of the Red Skinned people" used as a geographic label. **One documented exception:** a footnote points the reader to two Mayan sources, one of them a comparative work by authors inside that tradition. The tendency holds at six of seven and fails as a universal, and it should be stated at exactly that strength.

**Four internal positions the book never reconciles**, each of which any page drawing on that material must carry:

- **On presence.** *The Power of Now* is dismissed by name as "a misleading teaching," present-moment teaching is attacked at length as never leading anywhere — and then "live in the Now" is listed among the legitimate synonyms for direct cognition, the Now is affirmed as "the basic fundamental stuff of reality," and Eckhart Tolle is quoted approvingly with a page citation. Five positions.
- **On flow.** Sports highs and flow states are ruled out of samādhi in advance and the anticipated confusion called a "catastrophe" — then Csikszentmihalyi is quoted approvingly and at length, ordinary absorptions are read as unrecognised searches for samādhi, and "the flow state" is finally listed among the things "all in Buddhism." Four positions.
- **On the Dalai Lama.** The lineage is declared vacant from the Sixth's death onward, the present holder included — while the Seventh is quoted approvingly as an accurate summary of the Tantric path and the Fourteenth is cited as a doctrinal authority three separate times.
- **On the map.** Fifty-three graded stages are laid out and then declared "equivalent fabrications"; the transmutations of consciousness are said to be "only changes of appellation and not a change of substance"; and footnote 518 states the whole apparatus is unnecessary. This one the book does resolve, below the line, and the resolution is the two-truths distinction plus a stated pedagogical choice.

**Two duplicate models are printed without acknowledgement.** Nan Huai-Chin's list of the four formless absorptions omits the samādhi of Nothingness and adds an "infinite form" not in the standard scheme, thirty pages from the standard version. The ocean analogy for the eight consciousnesses is given twice with incompatible assignments, twenty pages apart. Both must be reported side by side, never merged.

**An evidential double standard.** The book demands that attainment claims be verified by a master, warns that phenomena cheat, and rejects claims that cannot be checked — then accepts anecdotal organ-transplant self-reports as evidence for a metaphysical claim, and cites a paranormal-media book as a source for what telepathy researchers believe.

**Three long-horizon science claims, `[n=3]`, and only one faces backwards.** Two to four hundred years for science to analyse the first two dhyānas (p 347) · two to three hundred years for the five elements (p 176) · and, looking back rather than forward, *"two thousand years later we have scientists finally catching up… they're simply putting footnotes on its body of teachings"* (p 536). The forward-facing pair are rare falsifiable statements from a book arguing that cultivation science is already complete and merely unread; the backward-facing one is the concordism habit in a different tense.

**One unsourced medical claim, `[DO NOT FILE]` as a claim.** p 189: *"through meditation you can even push out the decrepit jing-chi that would eventually cause cancer — which usually comes out through the feet, fingers or eyelids."* Recorded here as a source note and carried on no page. **Footnote 148 on the same page reads, in full: *See the various translations available of the Yellow Emperor's Classic of Internal Medicine*** — no edition, translator or page.

**Production.** Self-published and unedited. The title page reports 417,875 words and 608 pages, the file metadata 265,000 words and 377 pages, and the actual extraction 470,799 words and 673 pages — three different self-reported sizes. The back matter dates the book 2002; the title page 2003. A book the author names in one footnote as *White Fat Cow* is described in another as "yet unnamed and unpublished." **The converted file is missing six figures**, including the book's only synoptic chart of the samādhi and the heavens — no page may claim to present the full correspondence table without noting this.

**No case was found, across the ranges read, in which a source tradition's own account overturned the author's and his position had to change.** Every tradition the book handles supplies procedures; none supplies a verdict. Four instances make the shape unambiguous because in each the acceptance and the override sit inside a single passage: Patañjali's nir-vitarka and nir-vicāra kept as states and reclassified as a transition (p 364) · the ancient Taoist records honoured as autobiographical account while the practice built on them is called wrong (p 201) · the *Doctrine of the Mean* quoted twice and overruled between the quotations, prefaced with *even Confucianism correctly speaks of the proper road of cultivation* (p 502) · Zen's dismissal of gong-fu endorsed — *you can certainly dismiss gong-fu phenomena, and well you should* — and the school's grasp of its own dismissal called *a fault* within a hundred words (pp 199–200). ⚠ **Stated at range strength only.** This is an absence claim about the ranges read, not about the whole book; ranges not read support no claim either way.

**The book's own instrument for grading a text is dropped at the moment of judgement.** Texts are graded by the altitude at which their precision fails — the *Yoga Sūtras* are *a rudimentary classic of cultivation science* whose emphasis stops at the first two dhyāna, and the fact that the text *mentions* higher states is explicitly held not to count (p 364). That criterion is checkable and portable. When it comes to actually ranking Buddhism above yoga, it is replaced by an argument from later adoption — Vyāsa and Vācaspati Miśra having *tended to follow Buddhism's overall outline* (p 365) — which is equally consistent with prestige, institutional pressure or a better-organised presentation. The stronger instrument produces the reading; the weaker one produces the verdict. A related asymmetry is visible at pp 199–200, where thin recording is read as *original grandeur and purity* for Zen and as a low ceiling for other schools two paragraphs apart, with no stated rule for distinguishing refusal from inability.

**Conversion artefacts.** From roughly page 424 onward the PDF-to-markdown conversion interleaves quotations with their lead-ins, and in several places splices two or three authors into one apparent block. Attribution must be made by footnote number, never by proximity. A line beginning with a footnote number is not necessarily a footnote — three of the longest apparent footnotes in the file are misplaced body text. ⚠ **One badly-scrambled page sits well before that threshold: p 365**, where the sentence beginning *"Nevertheless, you should know that Patañjali's"* is severed from its continuation *"Yoga Sūtras identify this same stage of attainment…"* by two intervening paragraphs. Quotations from that page must be reassembled by eye.

---

## Claims Excluded From the Vault

The following are recorded here and enter no concept page:

An uncited Einstein endorsement of Buddhism, which appears twice · the one-percent-of-brain neuromyth · two statements of a doctrine that sexual innocence confers clairvoyance, one about girls at menarche and one about "virgin boys and girls" · Duncan McDougall's 1907 soul-weighing experiment offered as evidence that chi has weight · national and ethnic body-odour signatures, and a reading of young women's bodies as stagnant chi · "there is usually no way to reverse the effects of a drug once taken" · Native American trickster stories and peyote annexed to the yang-shen mechanism · a claim that people whose abilities come from spirit contact have lower IQ and visibly different eyes · an unexplained charge that form-based schools caused problems in "the countries they've invaded" · the reading of all war and national collapse as karmic retribution, separable from the remediability claim beside it · concordist claims that Śākyamuni anticipated wave-particle duality, the structure of galaxies and microorganisms · a claim about telepathy research sourced to a paranormal radio host · the assertion that Jesus and Mohammed "went to the East to learn."

**Added at the cluster R–U close.** The **shahāda retranslation** at p 480 — *al ilaha ill-Allah* declared *"usually incorrectly translated"* as "There is no God but Allah", with no Arabic, no citation and no acknowledgement of the standard sense; the mystical reading has genuine Sufi precedent and is carried as **Bodri's reading, `[CONTESTED]`**, while the translation-*fact* claim is not carried at all · the **Lincoln** and **Gandhi** claims (pp 647, 649), `[CONTESTED]`, carried as the author's readings only · **three named living practices used as illustrations of indoctrination with no engagement** — blood-transfusion refusal, refusal of physicians, and prohibitions on coffee or tea (p 600), plus the Sabbath light switch (p 601), **all belonging to traditions other than the author's, and no comparably specific Buddhist or Taoist example appears in the list** · the characterisation of esoteric practitioners as *"these unfortunates"* who have *"the wool pulled over their head"* (p 539) · the attribution of *"the refined elegance of the Japanese culture"* to Zen influx while disparaging the Esoteric schools' cultural effects (p 572) · the explanation of poverty and decline as *"their own lack of merit"* (p 617) · and **the ship-captain story at p 648**, recorded as the source's illustration and carried on no page as ethical instruction.

**Reportable only as what the source records, with the hazard stated and not reproduced at length:** a Tao-school practice of consuming one's own faeces after a sticky-rice fast, and the faeces of one's master if the stool is watery, together with a recommendation to drink one's first morning urine. No page presents any of this as practice.

**Reportable in full, never adopted:** the ranking of named historical figures on the ten bhūmis, which places Socrates around the third, Confucius at seven or eight, Nāgārjuna at the tenth, and Jesus and Mohammed at best "on the cusp" of the first — a judgment about the founders of two living traditions delivered without evidence, and one that violates the book's own rule, stated three paragraphs earlier, that no one can assess a stage above their own. The claim that the terminal attainment of Christianity, Islam and Hasidism sits at the Arhat's "one-sided and half-baked" halfway point belongs with it.

---

## Epistemic Notes

All claims drawn from this source carry `[POPULAR SOURCE]` or `[PARAPHRASED]` as appropriate, and doctrinal claims about any tradition are attributed to Bodri rather than to the tradition. Historical claims — Nāgārjuna as founder of the Esoteric school, Tibetan Buddhism as a Bon and Taoist admixture, qigong surviving the Cultural Revolution because it was materialist, the White Horse Monastery contest — are `[CONTESTED]` and reportable as the author's position only.

**One correction owed.** The book states that "until 1994 the American Psychiatric Association classified strong religious belief as a mental disorder," citing only "See the American Psychiatric Association DSM-IV 1994." That edition is the one that introduced a non-pathological category for religious and spiritual problems. The claim is `[CONTESTED]` pending verification and enters no page. The surrounding material on posthumous psychiatric diagnoses of mystics is unaffected and stands on its own.

**One testable prediction the corpus entails and never states.** The p 538 biconditional (*samādhi can only occur when the chi enters the central channel*) plus the p 582 dissolution signs together entail that **samādhi reports from channel-less traditions should still carry mirage, smoke, fireflies and lamp.** The literature is in print across several traditions and nobody appears to have counted. **This is the cheapest available test of the book's central mechanism** and it requires no attainment, no fieldwork and no access to the author.

**Where credit is due.** Bodri warns that the mercury in the *vajroli* protocol he reports is toxic, in the sentence after printing the protocol. He distinguishes pathological amenorrhoea, nutritional deficiency, stress, illness and xenoestrogen exposure from their cultivation look-alikes (p 123) — two hedges that foreclose genuinely dangerous misreadings. He states the cost of publishing the book — that cataloguing phenomena arms imposters and dilutes the teaching — accepts it, and proceeds. He records one documented change of mind, against his own teacher's position and to his own disadvantage. He hedges his own cosmological model at the point of use: *"Don't become too insistent upon this explanation as embodying truth"* — printing two pages of Dudjom Lingpa's five-colour cosmogony and then withdrawing it in two words, *"Not really."*

**And four more, all found in the closing clusters.** He reports **Tsong Khapa's own complaint that his tradition's manuals omit dosage, timing and injury avoidance** (p 557) — the negative-curriculum pattern testified from inside by the person best placed to know. He prints **a stopping rule** — *"if still no progress is forthcoming, prolonged application can incur dangerous obstacles"*, with a named retreat to the low junction (p 556) — a real safety instruction of a kind rare in this literature. He **offers three explanations of what the saṃbhogakāya is made of and withdraws all three**, including the Esoteric school's *"highly purified chi"*, which would have fitted his own energetics perfectly and cost nothing to adopt; the stated reason is that the available vocabulary is *"Desire Realm terminology."* And he **bars the magical reading of omniscience in the plainest language in the book**: *"if you think there is some samadhi where you know the number magically without any work, you haven't understood anything whatsoever"* (p 618) — closing a door every incentive in the genre pushed him to leave open.

**One further note on how he treats a hazardous passage.** Where he licenses hard conduct — *"a combination of saint and hero, Mafioso and thief"* (p 648) — **the karma is explicitly incurred and not excused**, which is more than most dirty-hands arguments concede. The guardrail is nonetheless made entirely of internal, unobservable, self-certified conditions, and the ship-captain story on the facing page dissolves the very remainder the guardrail depends on by framing a killing as compassion toward its victim. **Recorded as the source's illustration; carried on no page as ethical instruction.**

# Collision: Teaching Kills Sales vs. the Vault's Craft Corpus

## Source Tensions

- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/teaching-mode-kills-sales|Teaching Mode Kills Sales]] (Brunson) — content delivery prevents change; belief-breaking IS the teaching; giving real information on a webinar actively lowers conversion.
- The vault's entire creative-practice and craft corpus — e.g. [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/the-practice-is-the-thing|The Practice Is the Thing]], [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/get-all-the-knots-out-iteration|Get All the Knots Out]] — which assumes that real transmission of skill and understanding is the whole point, and that withholding the substance would be a failure of the craft.

## The Collision

Brunson says: if you actually teach people the thing, they leave satisfied and don't buy. So don't teach — break their beliefs, create the *desire* for the thing, and sell the teaching. Content given away for free on the webinar is a mistake; the webinar should change what people *believe*, not what they *know*.

The vault's craft corpus says the opposite with equal conviction: the value is in the transmission. A writing teacher who withheld the actual craft — who only made you *want* to write without showing you how — would be a fraud. The whole point of a craft tradition is that the substance passes from one person to the next. Withholding it isn't strategy; it's the betrayal of the thing.

These don't reconcile by saying "different contexts." They make opposite claims about what a teacher is *for*. Brunson: a teacher creates desire and sells fulfillment separately. The craft tradition: a teacher transmits capability, and creating desire without transmitting is manipulation.

## Candidate Idea

**Maybe the split is between two genuinely different things both called "teaching": desire-transmission and capability-transmission — and each is honest in one economy and a con in the other.**

Brunson isn't wrong that a webinar which fully teaches the method converts worse — that may be an empirical fact about human motivation. The craft tradition isn't wrong that withholding substance is a betrayal. They may both be right about different transactions: Brunson is running a *desire* economy (sell the wanting, deliver the capability later, for money), and the craft tradition runs a *capability* economy (the transmission is the gift, and desire is assumed).

**If true**: "teaching" is an ambiguous word hiding two incompatible activities, and a lot of the ugliness in the info-products world is desire-transmission wearing capability-transmission's clothes — selling the *wanting* while promising the *capability*. The genuinely unresolved question is whether it's possible to transmit capability freely and still sustain a business, or whether every teacher who needs to eat is pushed toward Brunson's model.

**If false**: one of them is straightforwardly right. Either Brunson's "teaching kills sales" is a rationalization for withholding value people paid for (and the craft tradition is correct that this is a betrayal), or the craft tradition is naive about motivation (and Brunson is correct that capability without desire is useless — you can hand someone the whole craft and they'll do nothing with it).

## What Would Need to Be True

For "two economies" to hold:
- Free full transmission would need to reliably fail to convert (Brunson's claim) AND reliably transmit capability to the few who act (the craft claim) — both true, different populations
- The tension would dissolve into "which economy are you in," not "who's right"

For "one is right" to hold:
- Either Brunson's paying customers would need to receive genuinely more capability than his free webinar attendees (justifying the withholding) — or they'd receive the same thing they could have gotten free, plus a bill (vindicating the craft critique)
- Or free-craft teachers would need to demonstrably produce more capable practitioners than desire-first sellers, or fewer

## Status

[x] Speculative  [ ] Being tested  [ ] Ready to promote

Genuinely unresolved, which is why it's filed rather than answered. Tests against: do Brunson's paid programs transmit more capability than his free content, or the same content gated? Can any craft teacher transmit freely and still eat? This bears directly on the newsletter's audience (creators deciding what to give away) and on the vault's own free-vs-paid posture.

# The Shadow That Somebody Else Trains For

## Source Tensions

- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/flow-states-are-not-samadhi|Flow States Are Not Samādhi]] — four positions across three hundred pages: flow as a genuine but lower shadow of absorption · its misidentification as *"another mistake you can make in elevating the lower to the higher"* · its pursuit as unrecognised samādhi-seeking · and Csikszentmihalyi quoted at length and approvingly
- Against: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/cross-domain/ki-no-nagashi-flow-state|Ki No Nagashi — Flow State]] — flow as a **trained terminal attainment** with a named prerequisite chain, an observable signature, and a failure mode
- And: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/measure-progress-by-clarity-not-by-the-body|Measure Progress by Clarity, Not by the Body]] — the corpus's own instruction to grade by mental clarity, which is the instrument the martial corpus is already using

## The Collision

Two corpora describe the same state and disagree about what kind of thing it is — not about its height on a ladder, but about whether it is a **by-product** or a **destination**.

**In the cultivation corpus, flow is downstream.** Training transforms the form skandha, the senses sharpen, and flow appears as a shadow of something real that lies further up. Nobody sets out for it. Anyone who mistakes it for the real thing has made a specific error, and the error has a stated remedy: study the definitions of the states properly so you can tell them apart.

**In the martial corpus, flow is the point, and it has a curriculum.** *Mushin* clears the analytical interference, ki gets developed, and *ki no nagashi* is the resulting condition in which it moves unobstructed. There is an entry sequence. There is an observable signature — economy, integration, responsiveness under high demand. There is even a named failure mode: being *bounced by* life rather than flowing through it. That is not the description of a by-product. That is the description of something people spend decades acquiring on purpose.

Here is why the disagreement isn't cosmetic. **The cultivation corpus's argument against pursuing flow is that pursuit of a by-product corrupts the path.** But the martial corpus has been pursuing it directly, with a method, and reporting the same signature — and its practitioners are not, on the cultivation corpus's own account, thereby stalled. Nobody in the martial material is described as arrested at the shadow. They are described as having arrived.

So one of three things is true, and the two corpora never meet to decide which.

| If… | Then… |
|---|---|
| They are the same state | Direct pursuit works, and the warning against elevating the lower to the higher is a warning about *naming*, not about practice |
| They are different states with one name | The corpora are talking past each other, and the martial *ki no nagashi* needs placing on the cultivation ladder before either claim means anything |
| The martial version is the shadow and its practitioners are stalled | Somebody has to say so, and nobody does |

**The uncomfortable detail is that the cultivation corpus supplies the instrument to settle it and doesn't use it.** Grade by clarity of mind, not by the state of the body. *Ki no nagashi* makes a clarity claim — the analytical layer relaxed, pattern-matching engaged, attention synchronised with breath and limb. That is a checkable description in exactly the currency the cultivation corpus says it wants. It is never checked.

## Candidate Idea

**A tradition that treats a state as a by-product will never build a curriculum for it, and will therefore never find out whether it was trainable.**

That is not a claim about which corpus is right. It is a claim about what each one is structurally able to discover. Classify a state as a shadow and the only research programme available is *warning people off it*. Classify it as a destination and you get an entry sequence, a signature, and a failure mode — which is to say, you get data.

The generalisation worth testing: **by-product classifications are self-sealing.** They remove the incentive to build the training path whose existence would refute them. And they are cheap to make, because a by-product needs no evidence to be dismissed — only a place lower on somebody's ladder.

`[n=2 SUGGESTIVE]`. The second instance is inside the cultivation corpus itself: bliss is classified as a motivational assist rather than an attainment, and no bliss curriculum follows, while the tantric material that *does* treat bliss as trainable produces a four-stage sequence. **The decisive test:** find a state that one corpus files as a by-product and another files as a destination, and check whether the by-product corpus has *any* method for producing it. If it turns out that by-product corpora routinely do have such methods, the candidate is wrong and the classification is doing no work.

## What Would Need to Be True

- **Placement, not polemic.** Somebody has to put *ki no nagashi* on the dhyāna ladder using the clarity criterion rather than the sensation criterion. The martial descriptions are detailed enough to try it. If it lands at or below the first rung, the cultivation corpus is vindicated and the collision closes.
- **The corpus's own census is the other half.** If genuine absorption is as rare as the corpus estimates — roughly thirty people worldwide with any dhyāna — and skilled martial practitioners reporting *ki no nagashi* number in the thousands, then either the states are different or the census is wrong. **Both corpora are on disk; this arithmetic has never been done.**
- **A named practitioner who has both.** The strongest evidence would be one person trained in both streams who reports whether entering *ki no nagashi* and entering the first dhyāna feel like the same door.

## Status

- [x] Speculative
- [ ] Being tested
- [ ] Ready to promote

**Next action:** the placement exercise above, run against `flow-states-are-not-samadhi` and `ki-no-nagashi-flow-state` together. Neither page currently links to the other, which is the first thing to fix whatever the outcome.

# One Perfect Thing — The Inverse Development Model

## The Capture
Itō Ittōsai. Founder of Ittō-ryū (one-sword school). Principle: you need exactly one technique if that technique is perfect. The school's name isn't about wielding one sword as a weapon — it's about one sword as a level of mastery. One thing, mastered to the point where all alternatives become redundant.

The resonance was immediate because it inverts the entire standard development model, and does it not as contrarianism but as someone who actually got there. He didn't have one technique because he ran out; he had one because he arrived.

## The Live Wire

- **First wire (obvious)**: More techniques = more options = better. The terminal state of development is maximum capability = maximum optionality. Itō Ittōsai says: the terminal state of development is one.

- **Second wire (deeper)**: This is only possible because the one technique, executed from genuine mushin and kime, is not predictable — there's no pattern to read, no telegraph from choice-making, no second-guessing. The apparent vulnerability of "one technique" is abolished by the absence of the self-monitoring layer that usually makes single-optionedness a trap. The one technique works because the person executing it has no hesitation, no alternative, no out. Pure commitment. That's not a limitation — that's a structural advantage.

- **Third wire (uncomfortable)**: Most people's "multiple options" is actually anxiety management. The backup plan is what prevents you from committing fully to the primary plan. The person with ten techniques has ten exit ramps. The person with one has none. Hitotsu no tachi forces you to ask: how many of your options are genuine capability and how many are psychological insurance?

## The Connection It Makes
- lovret-hyoshi-tactical-timing.md: hitotsu no tachi as the summit of the hyōshi chapter
- kokoro-shibumi-haragei-warrior-spirit.md: shibumi as the aesthetic version of the same principle — maximum effect from minimum means; shibumi and hitotsu no tachi are the same principle from aesthetic and tactical angles
- kime-focus-and-commitment.md: kime is the quality that makes hitotsu no tachi work — without total commitment, the one technique fails; with it, alternatives are redundant
- Polymathic OS (deliberate-experimentation.md): D5 is "small bets, fast feedback" — which is the OPPOSITE of hitotsu no tachi as development model. Interesting tension: experimental breadth in development vs. depth collapse at the end.

## What It Could Become

**Essay seed**: The piece nobody has written yet because they'd need to have read Lovret and the Polymathic OS in the same week is: "The development arc nobody talks about — why the person with ten tools at peak is actually behind the person with one. What Itō Ittōsai can teach about specialization vs. mastery that business advice cannot."

**Collision candidate**: Polymathic Breadth (D2 — cross-domain knowledge as combinatorial advantage) vs. Hitotsu No Tachi (one perfect thing at terminal development). These look like direct opposites. But they may operate at different stages: breadth in the middle game, collapse to one in the end game. Worth examining whether Simmons addresses this or if it's a genuine structural tension.

**Open question**: Is the hitotsu no tachi developmental model domain-general? What would "one thing mastered to the point where alternatives are redundant" look like in writing, leadership, teaching? And how would you know when you arrived vs. when you just stopped exploring out of laziness?

## Promotion Criteria
[ ] A second source touches this independently
[ ] Has survived two sessions without weakening
[x] The third wire (options as anxiety management) holds — this is the uncomfortable real claim
[ ] Has a falsifiable core claim

# Transgression as Intelligent Boundary Engineering — Not Rebellion

## The Capture

Selvalingam's frame for the left-hand path (vāmācāra) lands completely differently than the popular west reading: "The left-hand path is not rebellion against Brahmin orthodoxy. It's the deliberate, systematic violation of boundaries that have been established by right-hand practice. And it only works *after* the boundaries are rock-solid."

The distinction: Right-hand path builds unshakeable ground (guru connection, lineage transmission, devotional stability, ethical foundation). Only when that foundation is *immovable* can the left-hand path deliberately break boundaries without the practitioner shattering.

Example: Ramakrishna's two-phase sadhana. Phase 1 (right-hand): Puja, guru connection, bhakti, institutional practice. Years. Only then: Phase 2 (left-hand): Living as both man and woman, direct Bhairava sadhana, transgression of every social boundary. But he was *using* transgression as a tool, not fleeing from the structure.

The reversal: The west reads "transgression in spirituality" as the practitioner rejecting oppressive systems. The actual structure is: master the system perfectly, then deliberately violate it from a position of mastery.

## The Live Wire

**First wire (obvious):** Some spiritual traditions permit or require rule-breaking as part of practice. Left-hand path is one such tradition.

**Second wire (deeper):** Transgression only works when it's *intelligent boundary violation*, not reactive rebellion. Rebellion is the immature person fleeing structure. Intelligent violation is the masterful person *using* structure as a ladder and then burning the ladder while standing on something higher. The left-hand practitioner isn't breaking boundaries because they're oppressive — they're breaking them because they've built themselves to the point where the boundaries no longer contain them.

**Third wire (uncomfortable):** This means the person you think is "enlightened and free" (because they break rules) might just be a rebellious child using spiritual language. True left-hand practice requires the maturity/stability/groundedness that right-hand practice produces. And that means most people attempting left-hand path are actually just acting out. Which means most "enlightened" people teaching transgression are actually just sophisticated rebels.

## The Connection It Makes

This spark completely reframes [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/right-hand-left-hand-path-tantra|Right-Hand and Left-Hand Path]] — which documents the distinction but doesn't emphasize the prerequisite structure. But it also challenges [[ARCHIVES/concepts/cross-domain/spiritual-bypassing|Spiritual Bypassing]] — which frames spiritual practice as a potential escape from psychological work. The Tantric view: there's no shortcut; you do the right-hand work first, or left-hand work is just psychological material acted out as "transgression."

Cross-domain parallel: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/psychology/ego-development-theory-framework|Ego Development Theory]] — which also emphasizes that higher-stage capacities (like holding paradox, operating from multiple perspectives) are only available *after* earlier-stage development is complete. You can't jump to Strategist consciousness without moving through Expert and Achiever first. Same principle: structure first, freedom second.

## What It Could Become

**Essay seed:** Spiritual transgression as described in popular culture (the "enlightened guru who breaks rules") is almost always either (a) reactive rebellion mistaken for realization, or (b) genuine realization that required decades of foundational practice. There's no middle ground. This reframes every "guru scandal" through a clear lens: did this person complete right-hand development, or are they just a damaged person with philosophical language? The answer determines whether their transgression is wise/salvific or just destructive.

**Collision candidate:** [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/bhairava-and-bhairava-sadhana|Bhairava and Bhairava Sadhana]] — Bhairava is transgressive, fierce, boundary-breaking. But Selvalingam implies this is only *safe* after Shiva recognition (which requires right-hand work first). Does the vault's treatment of Bhairava practice adequately emphasize this prerequisite? Or does it allow for the reading that Bhairava practice can be undertaken without the right-hand foundation?

- [ ] Can articulate specific psychological/ethical criteria that determine "ready for left-hand practice" vs. "just acting out as transgression"

# Legend in Real Time

## The Capture
We picture myth as slow — a deed happens, decades pass, the embellishments accrete, and a few centuries later there's an epic. The Shivaji material breaks that picture. The sweetmeat-basket escape from Agra and Prataprao Gujar's suicidal charge with his "seven warriors" weren't mythologized by some distant later age. They became folk legend inside Shivaji's *own lifetime*, sung in his own country while the men involved were still alive or freshly dead. A Lata Mangeshkar song carries the seven-warriors story to this day — but the song is the late echo of a crystallization that happened almost immediately. The deed and its legend were nearly simultaneous.

## The Live Wire
- **First framing**: Famous escapes get romanticized.
- **Second framing**: The romanticizing was *contemporary*. There was no quiet century in which the facts cooled before the myth set. The legend formed in real time, which means the "true" version and the "sung" version were competing — or fusing — from almost the first telling.
- **Third framing**: This is the deeds wing and the construction wing meeting at the moment of formation. Usually the vault studies the deed (what happened) and the construction (how it was later made into meaning) as separated by time. Here they collapse into the same instant — which is exactly the hardest case for any historian, because there's no clean "before the legend" layer to recover. The fact arrives already mythologized.

## The Connection It Makes
Binds three pages across two warrants: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/the-sweetmeat-basket-escape|The Sweetmeat Basket Escape]] and [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/prataprao-gujar-and-the-charge-of-the-seven|Prataprao Gujar and the Charge of the Seven]] (deeds wing) meet [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/purandare-the-modern-myth-maker|Purandare the Modern Myth-Maker]] (construction wing) — the man who studies how the legend is *still* being made is downstream of legends that were made the instant the deeds happened.

## What It Could Become
**Essay angle**: "The Myth That Arrives On Time" — when does legend lag the event, and when does it form simultaneously? The hypothesis: legend crystallizes in real time when the deed is *witnessed and singable* (a basket, seven men, a charge) rather than administrative. The narratable deed mythologizes itself before the historian can get to it clean.

[ ] A second case of within-lifetime mythologization confirms the "narratable deed" pattern
[ ] Distinguishes genuine contemporary legend from later retrojection dressed as contemporary
[ ] Has a falsifiable core claim
